ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. text:
Corn grows best across a fairly wide temperature range, roughly 18-32°C, with an optimum around 25°C; growth outside this range is not well suited to the crop. For germination and early seedling establishment, soil temperature of about 12°C and above is adequate, while the optimum temperature range at flowering is roughly 26-30°C.

Low temperature is generally not a major limiting factor for corn production in Cambodia. However, high temperatures above about 38°C during March-April can be a constraint during early-wet-season (EWS) establishment, when the crop is most vulnerable, and this pattern can influence farmers' decisions about when to start planting.

Careful crop management -- correct planting depth, adequate soil cover, and good residue management -- can reduce the impact of temperature stress on establishment. In one upland trial, adding a crop-residue mulch layer to the soil surface (mulching) increased corn yield by 61% (from about 2.83 t/ha to 4.70 t/ha), partly attributed to more favourable soil temperature and moisture conditions at establishment; this same trial is discussed in more detail in the mulching cost-benefit topic.
